Pregnancy

Do pregnancy cravings or nausea predict a baby’s intelligence?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy cravings are not a test of a baby’s intelligence. Having none does not suggest poor development, and strong cravings do not promise exceptional ability. Understanding the difference between food preferences and nausea makes it easier to interpret claims about them and focus on the support you need.

Cravings, aversions and nausea describe different experiences

A food craving is a strong urge to eat a particular food, sometimes when you are not otherwise hungry. An aversion is a marked dislike of a food, taste or smell that may previously have been pleasant. Nausea means feeling sick and may occur with or without vomiting. Everyday language can group these experiences together, but they are not the same symptom.

You may have cravings without nausea, nausea without cravings, both or neither. That distinction matters when reading research: a study of vomiting cannot establish what a desire for chocolate means. No craving pattern is a required sign that a pregnancy is progressing well, and comparison with someone else’s symptoms is not a developmental assessment.

There is no single timetable or list of foods

Preferences can change early in pregnancy, and cravings are commonly reported during the second trimester. They may ease later, remain until birth or occasionally continue afterward. These are broad experiences rather than a schedule that every person must follow. A new or persistent difficulty eating deserves attention based on its effect on you, not simply on which trimester you are in.

Examples include fruit, sweet foods, chocolate, ice cream, salty snacks, pickled foods, meat or other protein foods, and substantial meals such as pizza. Some people want unusual combinations; others mainly avoid particular smells. None of these foods acts as a code for a baby’s intelligence. Familiarity, availability and personal preferences make any supposedly universal “most craved” list unreliable.

Hormones, smell and social context may all contribute

Researchers have proposed several explanations for cravings, and no single explanation covers every person. Pregnancy-related hormonal changes may alter appetite and the experience of taste or smell. A cooking smell that used to be ordinary may suddenly trigger queasiness, changing what feels possible to eat. Increased sensitivity does not make your nose a reliable food-safety detector.

Food traditions, family expectations, access and familiarity also influence what people want and how they describe it. Studies in particular communities can explore these influences, but cannot justify stereotypes about everyone of a nationality. Cultural influence also does not mean the experience is imaginary or deliberately produced. You can acknowledge a craving without treating it as a biological instruction.

A craving does not diagnose a deficiency or guarantee protection

The idea that the body asks for exactly the nutrient it lacks is appealing, but research does not support using an ordinary craving as a nutrient test. Wanting ice cream does not establish calcium deficiency, and wanting salt does not show a need to increase salt intake. A clinician assesses deficiency using diet, symptoms and appropriate tests, not the desired food alone.

Another proposed explanation is that aversions protect a pregnancy by steering people away from harmful substances. This remains a theory, not a dependable rule for choosing safe foods. You may dislike a nutritious food or crave something unsuitable. Keep following pregnancy food-safety advice and do not use a preference to decide that a risky product is safe. Non-food cravings require a separate conversation.

What the frequently cited intelligence study actually examined

A 2009 observational study assessed 121 mother–child pairs recruited through a pregnancy advice service. It compared children after pregnancies with nausea treated with doxylamine–pyridoxine, nausea without that treatment, and no nausea. At ages three to seven, the children completed tests of cognitive skills. All groups had IQ scores in the normal range.

Some measures of performance, language processing and memory were higher in the nausea-exposed groups. This was a small selected cohort, not an experiment showing that sickness improves a brain. Maternal IQ was also related to results. Most importantly for the craving question, food cravings were not the exposure being tested. The findings do not supply an intelligence prediction for an individual pregnancy.

Severe sickness is a reason for treatment, not a prediction

Mild to moderate pregnancy nausea and vomiting have not been shown to harm the baby. Severe sickness, including hyperemesis gravidarum, can prevent adequate drinking and eating and lead to dehydration, electrolyte disturbances or nutritional deficiencies. Some affected pregnancies need extra monitoring of fetal growth. Those concerns support getting care; they do not establish that your child’s future intelligence has been reduced.

Contact your maternity team if you cannot drink enough, are passing very little or dark urine, feel faint, are losing weight or cannot keep essential medicine down. Ask for help when symptoms interfere with everyday life as well. Treatment may include anti-sickness medicine, fluids and nutritional support. Do not preserve or prolong nausea in the hope of a cognitive benefit.

Work with the foods you can manage

When eating is manageable, aim for variety across the day: sources of carbohydrate, protein, fruit or vegetables, and suitable dairy foods or alternatives. A desired sweet or salty snack does not need to become your entire diet or a source of guilt. Regular meals and accessible snacks can make it easier to include what you enjoy alongside other nourishment.

If smells or sickness limit intake, try small portions of tolerated foods and drinks, then broaden the range as you improve. For example, discuss another protein source if meat is difficult, or an appropriate calcium-containing alternative if milk is unappealing. A dietitian can help when several foods or whole groups are excluded. During severe sickness, preserving fluids and finding tolerable nutrition takes priority over meeting an idealized menu.

Tell your maternity team about non-food cravings

An urge to eat soil, clay, chalk, soap or other non-food substances is often called pica. Repeatedly craving or chewing ice can also be worth mentioning. Pica can be associated with iron deficiency, although the urge does not prove a deficiency or identify the correct treatment. Tell your midwife or doctor without embarrassment so they can consider blood tests and support.

Do not eat non-food substances to satisfy the craving: some contain toxins or infectious material or can injure the digestive tract. If you have swallowed a potentially harmful substance, contact poison advice or urgent care and describe what and how much you took. Do not induce vomiting. Keep supplements to the plan recommended for you rather than adding high doses based on a craving.

Development depends on more than a pregnancy symptom

A child’s learning and development reflect many interacting genetic, health and environmental factors. Neither the presence nor the absence of a craving provides a useful measure of those future abilities. There is no particular craving to achieve, and no food or supplement in this discussion can promise an especially intelligent baby.

Continue antenatal appointments, use the supplements advised for your circumstances and raise problems with intake or wellbeing. If an intelligence claim has made you anxious, ask your maternity clinician to discuss it. Practical support for your health now is more useful than judging a pregnancy by how dramatic its symptoms feel. A healthy pregnancy can include very different experiences of food.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Observational research on nausea must not be presented as proof that cravings predict intelligence.

Manage severe sickness and nutritional difficulty; do not encourage symptoms or imply that a parent has determined future ability.

How BeMama can help

Choose one practical next step, such as finding a tolerated meal alternative or telling your maternity team about persistent sickness.

When to seek help

Inability to maintain fluids, faintness, very little urine or rapid weight loss needs medical advice. Seek poison advice for potentially harmful swallowed substances.

  • RCOG — Pregnancy sickness and hyperemesis gravidarum

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Cravings, aversions and nausea are distinct experiences.
  • Their presence or absence cannot predict an individual child’s intelligence.
  • An ordinary craving does not diagnose a vitamin or mineral deficiency.
  • Severe sickness and non-food cravings deserve support and assessment.
  • Varied, tolerable nutrition and routine antenatal care matter more than a symptom-based prediction.

Frequently asked questions

I have no cravings. Does that mean something is wrong?

No. Cravings vary between people and pregnancies and are not required for healthy development. Keep your usual antenatal care and discuss any separate concerning symptoms with your maternity team.

Did the intelligence study actually examine food cravings?

No. It examined nausea and vomiting, treatment exposure and later cognitive test scores. It cannot establish what a particular food craving means for a baby’s intelligence.

Does more vomiting mean a smarter baby?

No. The research does not provide an individual prediction or show that inducing or prolonging sickness helps development. Severe vomiting can cause medical problems and should be treated.

Should I avoid anti-sickness medicine because of this claim?

No. Discuss a suitable treatment with your clinician. Do not leave significant symptoms untreated in pursuit of an unproven benefit or stop prescribed medicine without advice.

Does craving ice cream mean I need calcium tablets?

Not by itself. A preference for a food is not a deficiency test. Discuss your overall intake and use supplements recommended for your circumstances rather than adding high doses.

Why do I dislike foods I used to enjoy?

Changes in taste, smell and nausea can make familiar foods unpleasant. The exact causes are not fully understood. A dietitian or maternity clinician can suggest alternatives if your intake becomes restricted.

Can I eat the sweet or salty food I want?

Often a portion can fit alongside other foods, provided it is safe for pregnancy and compatible with your own medical advice. A craving does not make a food compulsory or remove the need for variety.

What if I want to eat soil or chalk?

Tell your maternity team and avoid eating it. Non-food cravings can be associated with iron deficiency and deserve assessment. Seek poison advice if you have already swallowed something potentially harmful.

Will a period of poor eating determine my child’s abilities?

You cannot make that prediction from a difficult week or an episode of sickness. Get help with persistent restricted intake, dehydration or weight loss; support and treatment are the useful next steps.

Should cravings stop at a particular week?

There is no compulsory timetable. They can change across pregnancy and sometimes persist afterward. Ask for help whenever they interfere with adequate nutrition, safety or daily life.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
